synthesis.headline: The block's endgame is complete: a cutoff low over the upper Midwest anchors a central-and-eastern rain-and-severe corridor while the heat ridge settles into its Desert Southwest home
synthesis.narrative:
The multi-week summer block Tlaloc has tracked into its endgame has now finished its transition. Today's 500 mb analysis shows a robust western ridge firmly centered over the Desert Southwest and Great Basin (a 601 dam closed high near Nevada/southern California) opposite a deep, unseasonably amplified late-summer trough running from the northern Plains through the central Mississippi Valley, with a genuine cutoff low pinched off over the upper Midwest near the Illinois-Indiana line. This is an amplified ridge-trough dipole, not a Rex block: there is no closed cyclone stacked poleward of the ridge. The cutoff and the frontal systems draped beneath it are the day's engine. This is the third day of the ridge's southwestward retreat, and the severe corridor has marched east with it — from the Missouri/Illinois region two days ago to the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys today.

Today's busiest center of action is the eastern half of the country. A well-organized extratropical cyclone sits over the Ohio Valley-Great Lakes border on satellite, with its trailing cold front sweeping through the mid-Mississippi Valley and a separate Gulf Coast low (near 1008-1011 mb) parked over a deep moist-tropical airmass with upper-70s dewpoints from east Texas through the Southeast. SPC carries a Slight Risk across the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys, damaging wind the primary hazard under 35 kt shear, with an isolated tornado threat near the surface low and triple point over Indiana and Kentucky where destabilization allows. WPC overlays a broad Slight Risk for excessive rainfall from the Great Lakes through the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys into the Southeast, Gulf Coast, and southern High Plains, with localized flash flooding, and that threat translates eastward toward the Mid-Atlantic and New England by Monday. Canada carries real weight in the story: a strong 1038 hPa high over the Hudson Bay/Ungava region tightens the gradient across the western interior provinces, while the Day 2 picture brings an intense upper low from Alberta into Saskatchewan with a 50-70 kt 500 mb jet spreading into the northern High Plains — the leading edge of a genuinely progressive northern-tier flow.

Aloft the story is coherent. Air Mass RGB shows the cyclone's tight cyclonic curl and cold conveyor near the Ohio Valley, with a compact high-PV dry-intrusion tongue wrapping from the central Plains into the lower Mississippi and Tennessee corridors on the cyclonic, trough side of the flow. A sharp airmass boundary from the central Plains southwestward marks the implied jet corridor. Importantly, the broad red-orange over the central and southern Plains west of that tongue is warm, dry mid-to-upper tropospheric air under the downstream ridge — not a stratospheric feature — given its extent and its distance from the trough axis. The regime question is settled by the ensemble pair. The 6-10 day (Aug 5-9) keeps the western positive anomaly modest (roughly +3 to +6 dam) with its zero line back near the central Prairies and upper Midwest, and a deep cold low anchored over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago; the 8-14 day (Aug 7-13) re-consolidates the ridge but plants its core over the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico, leaving the northern Plains and Canadian Prairies in a below-normal trough regime on the cyclonic side of the Arctic low. Between the two leads the ridge contracts further southwest toward its climatological home while the north stays cool — a genuine geographic retreat, not a cosmetic flattening and not a collapse. The 6-10 day temperature outlook corroborates, anchoring the hottest 90-100% probabilities over the Great Basin, southern Rockies, and central/southern Plains while the northern tier and Great Lakes weaken. The teleconnection indices are a directional cross-check, not the basis: a rising PNA (+0.74) fits western ridging/eastern troughing, and a strongly positive AO (+1.23) fits the open, progressive polar flow and the deep-but-unblocked Arctic low — though summer signals are weak and secondary to the height field.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-summer North America, with heat-and-severe season driving both the entrenched interior warmth beneath the retreating ridge and the marginal severe threats ringing it, and the North American Monsoon in full swing over the Four Corners and New Mexico feeding the southern High Plains flash-flood and severe-wind threat. The ENSO backdrop remains one of steady cold-to-warm transition: after a weak La Niña through late 2025 (SON 2025 ONI -0.51), anomalies warmed through neutral in early 2026 and reached +0.98 by April-June, indicating a developing El Niño that will increasingly shape steering and shear into the back half of the season. The hurricane basins stay split against the climatological ramp toward the September peak — the Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf are quiet with no development expected over the next seven days, while the East Pacific holds Tropical Storm Genevieve west of the southern Baja California peninsula, with no additional formation anticipated.
synthesis.regional_notes: No SPC mesoscale discussions are active. Today's sharpest sub-synoptic signal is the damaging-wind and isolated-tornado threat near the surface low and triple point over Indiana and northern/east-central Kentucky, alongside a flash-flood axis running the Ohio and Tennessee Valley corridor into the Gulf states; isolated severe wind gusts are also possible over the southern High Plains, New Mexico, and southeast Arizona from diurnal heating and steep lapse rates. Looking to Sunday, SPC drops to a Marginal Risk from the upper Ohio Valley into the Carolinas and Georgia (mainly damaging winds along the front and a lifting warm front), plus a conditional late-night hail threat over North Dakota and far northwest Minnesota as the Alberta-to-Saskatchewan upper low erodes the cap ahead of the advancing cold front. In Canada, the 1038 hPa Hudson Bay high holds the tightest gradient across the western interior provinces.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 1200Z 1 August 2026 WPC analysis shows a broad high-pressure complex dominating much of the central and western interior, with several centers in the 1018-1022 mb range from the northern Rockies eastward through the central Plains — individually unremarkable for early August, and collectively producing a slack gradient across most of the West and central CONUS. The most dynamically relevant surface feature is a low near the central Gulf Coast region reading near 1008-1011 mb, with an associated cold front trailing southwestward and a warm front or stationary boundary extending eastward along the Gulf states, and this frontal zone is the primary moisture focus — dewpoints in the upper 70s F are visible along and ahead of it from eastern Texas through the Southeast. A second, sharper cold front extends from a low near the northern Great Lakes southward through the mid-Mississippi Valley, with a pronounced dew point contrast on either side and stations ahead of it in the Ohio Valley still showing mid-70s moisture; this boundary is the most credible lift-focusing feature east of the Rockies. Along the Pacific Coast, a 1013 mb low sits off the California coast with the implied onshore gradient consistent with a marine layer push, while a 1008 mb low is analyzed near the Alaska panhandle. Pressure gradients are tightest around the Great Lakes low and along the Gulf Coast frontal zone; the interior West shows very slack gradients, leaving any convective development there dependent on the upper-level pattern and terrain rather than the surface pressure field.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This is a CMC surface analysis valid 00Z Saturday 1 August 2026, on a polar stereographic projection whose upper frame covers the high Arctic and pole rather than the populated south. The most prominent Canadian feature is a strong high of 1038 hPa centered over what appears to be Hudson Bay or the Ungava Peninsula region, with tightly packed isobars on its western flank implying a sharp pressure gradient across the western interior provinces; that gradient, combined with a quasi-stationary or slow-moving frontal boundary trailing southwestward from a low analyzed near the Great Lakes region at roughly 999-1001 hPa, suggests focused low-level convergence and lift along a corridor running from the central prairies toward the Ontario-Manitoba border area. A separate low complex labeled around 997-1001 hPa sits over what the visible coastlines suggest is the northeastern North Atlantic or Labrador Sea, with frontal boundaries extending southward and connecting to the Atlantic seaboard pattern over the northeastern United States. Along the Canada-US border in the west, a broad 1010-1016 hPa high-pressure ridge bridges British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest, consistent with subsidence suppressing precipitation there. Tropical Storm Genevieve is annotated at 22.4N 130.7W in the lower left, well into the eastern North Pacific and not an immediate Canadian concern, but its associated moisture feed could eventually interact with the mid-latitude pattern along the BC coast.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: This 500 mb analysis valid 1200 UTC 1 August 2026 shows a high-amplitude longwave pattern with a deep trough axis running roughly from the northern Plains southward through the central Mississippi Valley, with 500 mb heights falling to around 576–579 dam along the trough axis and the 570 dam contour pushed well southward into the south-central states, indicating an unseasonably amplified late-summer trough for early August. The western ridge is robust, centered over the Desert Southwest and Great Basin where the 601 dam closed high (the blue H) sits over approximately Nevada or southern California, and the ridge axis extends northward into the Pacific Northwest; this is a separate feature from the trough and the two together form a classic amplified ridge-trough dipole rather than a Rex block, since there is no closed low stacked meridionally beneath or poleward of the ridge. The red L over the upper Midwest, positioned near the Illinois-Indiana region, appears to be a closed 500 mb low near the 576–578 dam level, making it a genuine cutoff low that has separated from the main westerly flow; its tilt is difficult to determine with certainty from the height contours alone, but the orientation of surrounding contours suggests a neutral to slightly negative tilt. The green shading, which by College of DuPage convention represents relatively cool temperatures at 500 mb, is concentrated within and just downstream of the trough, consistent with the cold core structure of the cutoff. The overall pattern looks blocked or at minimum strongly retrogressive given the anchored western ridge and the stalled cutoff low, rather than a progressive zonal flow regime.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 AirMass RGB from 01 Aug 2026 at 13:51Z shows a well-organized extratropical cyclone centered near the Ohio Valley-Great Lakes border region, identifiable by the tight cyclonic curl of cloud wrapping into a cold conveyor belt head, with deep bright-white convective tops arching across the upper Midwest into the Great Lakes. A sharp, high-contrast airmass boundary runs from roughly the central Plains southwestward, separating the deep orange-red dry air to the west and northwest from the moist green signature to the east and south; this boundary marks the implied jet corridor and leading edge of a dry intrusion that wraps cyclonically around the western and southern flanks of the trough. The dry intrusion itself appears as a compact, elongated tongue of saturated orange-red streaming from the central Plains into the lower Mississippi Valley and eastward toward the Tennessee corridor, consistent with a high-PV stratospheric-intrusion signature on the cyclonic, trough-side of the flow rather than a broad ridge signature. The Gulf of Mexico and southeastern states display the expected deep moist-green tropical airmass, with scattered white convective cells visible along the Florida peninsula and offshore in the western Atlantic. The broad red-orange colors over the central and southern Plains west of the dry intrusion tongue are likely warm, dry mid-to-upper tropospheric air under a downstream ridge rather than a stratospheric feature, given their spatial extent and position away from the cyclone.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: The dominant feature across the broad tropics and subtropics from the eastern Pacific through South America is a deep green expanse indicating moist tropical air at mid to upper levels, consistent with the August ITCZ and active convective season; scattered clusters of bright white high-topped convection are visible over Central America, the western Caribbean, and the Colombian and Venezuelan coastlines. A sharp airmass boundary runs across southern Canada from the Canadian Rockies toward the Great Lakes, where orange-brown tones indicative of drier upper-tropospheric air give way northward to darker blue-green hues marking colder upper-level air over the Canadian interior, and this boundary implies the polar jet corridor along that transition zone. Over the high latitudes of northern Canada and the visible Arctic margin, the darker blue coloring indicates cold dry upper-tropospheric air consistent with the poleward airmass. Two vigorous extratropical systems are clearly visible in the Southern Hemisphere westerlies south of roughly 50°S, one near the tip of South America and another farther south, each showing the classic comma-cloud structure in white with flanking deep red-orange dry intrusions on their poleward and western flanks — these compact, elongated red tongues wrapping cyclonically around the system centers are consistent with high-PV stratospheric-intrusion signatures rather than broad ridge subsidence. No clearly organized tropical wave or named storm structure is evident in the Atlantic or eastern Pacific basins at this time, though the convective clusters near Central America and the southern Caribbean warrant attention.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a broad above-normal temperature signal covering virtually the entire contiguous United States, with the highest probabilities, reaching the 90-100% range, centered over a roughly elliptical core spanning the central Great Basin through the southern Rockies and extending eastward across the central and southern Plains into Oklahoma and northern Texas. A secondary 90-100% core sits across the Florida peninsula and immediate Gulf Coast. Probabilities step down to 70-80% across much of California, the Pacific Northwest, the Upper Midwest, and the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast, leaving only a narrow corridor near the Great Lakes and northern New England where probabilities fall to the 40-50% leaning-above range, the weakest warm signal on the continental map. No below-normal signal appears anywhere in the contiguous US. In Alaska, the interior and south-central panhandle show a 40-50% above-normal signal while the western and southwestern mainland carry below-normal probabilities at 33-40%, suggesting a split pattern there; the Aleutians show a similar east-above, west-below structure. The geographic extent and magnitude of the warm probabilities over the West and central US are consistent with a persistent, amplified upper-level ridge anchored over the Intermountain West continuing well into the 6-10 day window rather than breaking down, though the chart plots probabilities only and does not directly show the upper-level pattern.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast valid 6–10 August 2026, consistent with a CPC ensemble-mean product. Heights are contoured in dam at 60 m intervals; anomalies are the dashed lines, with blue dashed for negative and red dashed for positive departures.

The dominant feature is a strong negative height anomaly centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and northern Baffin Island region, where the blue dashed contours reach approximately -120 dam — that reading is almost certainly a misread or a units issue; the anomaly contour interval on CPC 6-10 day products is typically 6 dam, so the innermost blue contour there more plausibly represents a departure near -12 dam, which would itself be a pronounced cold anomaly. The associated absolute-height low is centered near the same area with a closed contour around 534–540 dam, representing a deep, cold upper low over the high Arctic. Across the contiguous United States and northern Mexico, the absolute heights reach 582–594 dam, and the red dashed anomaly lines show a modest positive departure (roughly +3 to +6 dam) extending from the southwestern U.S. into the central Plains, but the zero-anomaly line cuts through roughly the central Canadian Prairies and the upper Midwest, meaning any positive anomaly over the interior West is confined well south of its typical ridge position and is not particularly amplified. The 500 mb ridge axis over western North America runs roughly north-northwest to south-southeast from British Columbia toward the Desert Southwest, but given the positive anomalies are modest and limited in northern extent, the pattern implies a relatively progressive, only weakly amplified western ridge with the flow trending toward a more zonal character across the mid-latitudes of the U.S., rather than a sustained western ridge amplification.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb height and height anomaly (DNS = departures from normal, dashed contours) ensemble-mean prognostic valid 8–14 August 2026, made 31 July 2026 — consistent with a CPC 8–14 day product. The dominant feature is a deep cold-core low centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with closed height contours near 5040 dam and a strong negative height anomaly there (the dashed red contours surrounding the low indicate below-normal heights, on the order of several dam below normal given the contour interval). Downstream, the height pattern over the contiguous United States shows a broad, amplified ridge, with the 5940 dam contour reaching into the central and southern Rockies/southern Plains area and the highest contours in the western CONUS domain sitting near the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico rather than over the northern Rockies or northern Plains — the ridge axis has retreated well southward, meaning western Canada and the northern Plains lie in a below-normal height regime on the cyclonic side of the polar trough rather than under a positive anomaly. The positive height anomaly center for the CONUS ridge appears anchored near the central and southwestern U.S., not over the northern Rockies, while the northern Plains and Canadian Prairies sit in the negative anomaly field extending southward from the Arctic low. Over the eastern CONUS and western Atlantic, heights trend back toward near-normal to slightly below normal, with the trough axis implied by the cyclonic curvature of the contours running roughly through the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley region.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Low pressure over the Middle Mississippi Valley moves eastward to the Eastern Ohio Valley by Monday, triggering showers and severe thunderstorms across Ohio and Tennessee Valleys. Slight Risk (2/5) for severe thunderstorms Saturday; Slight Risk (2/4) for excessive rainfall Saturday through Monday over Great Lakes, Ohio Valley, Tennessee Valley, Southeast, Gulf Coast, and Southern Rockies/Southern High Plains. Heavy rain will produce localized flash flooding in urban areas, small streams, and low-lying zones. On Sunday, a boundary over Lower Great Lakes brings additional heavy rain. By Monday, storms extend from Northeast to Gulf Coast with heavy rain over Northern Mid-Atlantic and New England. Northwest Coast frontal system produces scattered rain Saturday-Sunday; showers and thunderstorms develop over Northern Plains Monday.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: SLIGHT RISK issued for Ohio and Tennessee Valleys. A positive-tilt mid-level trough and surface low moving east-southeastward will support thunderstorm development this afternoon into evening. Damaging winds are the primary severe threat due to strong shear (35 kt over Kentucky/Indiana/Ohio, 20-25 kt over Tennessee Valley). Isolated tornado risk possible near the surface low and triple point across Indiana and northern/east-central Kentucky, pending adequate destabilization. Isolated severe wind gusts also expected in southern High Plains, New Mexico, and southeast Arizona due to diurnal heating, strong upper winds, and steep lapse rates. Uncertainty remains regarding northward extent of warm sector and destabilization progression northward.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No mesoscale discussions currently active. Storm Prediction Center is not monitoring any organized convective threat at this time.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days across the Atlantic, Caribbean, or Gulf of America.

East Pacific: Tropical Storm Genevieve is currently active west of the southern Baja California Peninsula tip, under NHC advisory. No additional tropical cyclone formation expected in the eastern and central North Pacific over the next 7 days.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: Current ENSO phase is La Niña, with the most recent index (SON 2025) at -0.51°C anomaly. The cold phase is weakening through early 2026, with anomalies trending toward neutral by late winter (JFM: -0.14°C). A transition to warm conditions appears likely by spring 2026, with the MAM outlook showing +0.51°C anomaly and AMJ reaching +0.98°C, suggesting an emerging El Niño phase by late spring.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA rising sharply to +0.74 (7-day mean), trending from +0.44 last week. Latest daily value +0.07, but the preceding week showed sustained positive values (+0.69 to +1.41), supporting western North American ridging with eastern troughing. AO strongly positive at +1.23 and +0.95 (7-day), up from +0.22 last week, favoring open polar flow rather than high-latitude blocking. NAO swung decisively positive to +0.71 (7-day mean) from -0.49, currently +0.58, suggesting Atlantic systems will flow eastward more readily. Summer teleconnections are directionally weaker; treat these as supporting signals rather than definitive.
